reference.source: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: A heterogeneous group of disorders characterised by loose, inelastic, sagging skin that hangs in redundant folds and does not recoil when stretched
It may be inherited or acquired; inherited forms include autosomal dominant (often ELN), autosomal recessive, and X-linked (occipital horn) types with differing systemic risks
Unlike Ehlers-Danlos syndrome the skin is lax rather than hyperextensible, and joint hypermobility is not the dominant feature
Systemic elastic-tissue involvement can cause emphysema, aortic and arterial aneurysm or tortuosity, and hollow-viscus diverticula depending on subtype
Autosomal recessive and some syndromic forms may include developmental delay, growth restriction, and skeletal anomalies
Acquired cutis laxa can follow inflammatory skin disease, drug reactions, or systemic conditions and may be a marker of underlying disease
Diagnosis combines the clinical appearance, skin biopsy showing sparse or fragmented elastic fibres, and molecular genetic testing to define the subtype
Management is supportive, with cardiorespiratory and vascular surveillance in at-risk subtypes and plastic-surgical options for the skin
reference.pathophysiology: Cutis laxa reflects a defect in the formation, cross-linking, or maintenance of elastic fibres in connective tissue. Inherited forms disrupt elastin itself (for example ELN variants) or proteins and enzymes required for elastic-fibre assembly, copper-dependent cross-linking, or intracellular trafficking, leaving elastic fibres sparse, fragmented, or disorganised. Loss of functional elastic tissue removes the normal recoil of the skin and can weaken the walls of the lungs, arteries, and hollow organs, explaining the sagging skin together with emphysema, arterial aneurysm and tortuosity, and diverticula in the more severe systemic subtypes. Acquired forms arise from elastic-fibre destruction driven by inflammation or other secondary insults.
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with elastic-tissue staining to assess elastic-fibre number and structure
Molecular genetic testing with a cutis laxa gene panel to define the subtype
Echocardiography and vascular imaging for aneurysm and arterial tortuosity
Pulmonary function testing and chest imaging for emphysema
Developmental and growth assessment in children
Investigation for an underlying cause when an acquired form is suspected
redFlags: Acute chest, back, or abdominal pain suggesting arterial aneurysm rupture or dissection
Progressive breathlessness from emphysema or spontaneous pneumothorax
Signs of bowel or bladder diverticular complications
New neurological signs suggesting cerebrovascular involvement
Rapidly progressive acquired skin laxity indicating serious underlying disease
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies widely by subtype: isolated cutaneous disease is mainly a cosmetic and functional concern with a normal lifespan, whereas forms with pulmonary, cardiovascular, or multisystem involvement can significantly reduce life expectancy. Surveillance of at-risk systems guides outcome.
pitfalls: Confusing lax, non-recoiling skin with the hyperextensible skin of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
Treating it purely as a cosmetic problem and missing systemic elastic-tissue disease
Failing to arrange cardiovascular and pulmonary surveillance in high-risk subtypes
Overlooking an underlying systemic trigger in acquired cutis laxa
Not defining the subtype, which is essential for prognosis and counselling
